rules.quote: Use adjectives sparingly and only when they are essential for meaning.
rules.specification: Interpret ‘essential’ and ‘critical’ semantically, not as a numerical limit on adjectives. An adjective is unnecessary when removing it preserves the intended substantive meaning. Repetition of an inherent property is an explicit case.
rules.violation_condition: An adjective adds no essential meaning, including when it merely repeats a quality or property inherent in its noun.
when: Includes adjectives that repeat a quality or property already inherent in the noun.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: unnecessary adjectives and inherent-property repetition are consolidated into one essential-meaning check rather than producing overlapping findings.

rules.quote: A compound adjective usually has a hyphen if the adjective is before the noun it is describing.
rules.specification: Resolve ‘usually’, ‘most’ and the unspecified lexical exceptions through a dictionary-backed exception list. The primary finding is a missing hyphen; the ‘-ly’ exception can instead produce an unwanted-hyphen finding.
rules.violation_condition: A compound adjective before its noun lacks its normally required hyphen, or a compound construction contains a hyphen joining an adverb ending in ‘-ly’ where that construction normally takes no hyphen.
when: Compound adjectives normally take a hyphen before the noun they describe.
A compound used after its noun can be unhyphenated; the page does not establish a universal prohibition on post-nominal hyphens.
Most constructions containing an adverb ending in ‘-ly’ take no hyphen.
Lexical exceptions exist.
rules.why: G-2: noun position and ‘-ly’ constructions change when the same compound-hyphen check applies; they are not separate overlapping checks.

covers.quote: There is a common order for strings of adjectives
Write strings of adjectives in an order that creates a more natural-sounding English.
evaluative – features of a noun that you can measure or compare
descriptive – features of a noun that you can’t measure
definitive – features of a noun that are intrinsic to the noun.
Evaluative adjectives can also express an opinion.

examples.note: The adjectives are evaluative, descriptive and definitive respectively.

parts.quote: A beautiful round committee table

rules.violation_condition: A string of adjectives places a descriptive adjective before an evaluative adjective, or a definitive adjective before an evaluative or descriptive adjective modifying the same noun.
when: Applies when adjectives of different types modify the same noun.
The required type order is evaluative, descriptive, definitive.
No additional ordering within a type is stated.
rules.why: G-4: the body introduces the actionable ordering; its introductory wording and category definitions belong to that single check.

covers.quote: no commas between adjectives of different types
no commas and no ‘and’ before definitive adjectives.
You can also use ‘and’ instead of commas to help the sentence flow more smoothly.

examples.note: The page identifies ‘large’ and ‘black’ as descriptive and ‘nuclear’ as definitive.

parts.quote: A large, black nuclear submarine

examples.note: The page identifies ‘new’ and ‘red’ as descriptive and the remaining modifiers as definitive.

parts.quote: A new, red long-range electric car

examples.note: The example illustrates the permission to use ‘and’ instead of a comma.

parts.quote: A new and shiny red long-range electric car

rules.quote: commas between adjectives of the same type
rules.violation_condition: An adjective string lacks a comma between same-type non-definitive adjectives that are not joined by ‘and’, contains a comma between different adjective types, or contains a comma before a definitive adjective.
when: Applies to strings of adjectives modifying the same noun.
Commas separate adjectives of the same type, except before definitive adjectives.
Commas do not separate adjectives of different types.
‘And’ may replace a comma to improve flow, but this permission does not extend to definitive adjectives.
rules.why: G-2 consolidates the type-dependent comma cases; G-3 records ‘and’ as an exception to the comma requirement rather than a separate positive rule.

rules.violation_condition: ‘And’ is used as an adjective-string separator immediately before a definitive adjective.
when: Applies to definitive adjectives within strings modifying the same noun.
rules.why: This checks a conjunction, not comma placement, so it produces a different finding from the comma rule.
